{{Short description|Quantum consistency equation}}
In [[physics]], the '''Yang–Baxter equation''' (or '''star–triangle relation''') is a [[consistency equation]] which was first introduced in the field of [[statistical mechanics]]. It depends on the idea that in some scattering situations, particles may preserve their momentum while changing their quantum internal states. It states that a matrix <math> R</math>, acting on two out of three objects, satisfies

<math display=block>(\check{R}\otimes \mathbf{1})(\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R})(\check{R}\otimes \mathbf{1}) =(\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R})(\check{R} \otimes \mathbf{1})(\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}),</math>

where <math>\check{R}</math> is <math>R</math> followed by a swap of the two objects. In one-dimensional quantum systems, <math>R</math> is the [[S-matrix|scattering matrix]] and if it satisfies the Yang–Baxter equation then the system is [[Integrable system#Quantum integrable systems|integrable]]. In quantum integrable models, the Yang–Baxter equation ensures that multi-particle scattering processes can be factorized into a sequence of two-body interactions, preserving exact solvability.<ref>{{cite book |last=Baxter |first=R. J. |title=Exactly Solved Models in Statistical Mechanics |publisher=Academic Press |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-12-083180-7}}</ref> The Yang–Baxter equation also shows up when discussing [[knot theory]] and the [[braid group]]s where <math> R</math> corresponds to swapping two strands. Since one can swap three strands in two different ways, the Yang–Baxter equation ensures that both paths are the same.

{{Dark mode invert|[[File:Illustration of Yang Baxter Equation.png|thumb|Illustration of the Yang–Baxter equation]]}}

==History==
According to [[Michio Jimbo]],<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Jimbo
| first = M.
| title = Introduction to the Yang-Baxter Equation
| journal = International Journal of Modern Physics A
| publisher = World Scientific
| volume = 4
| issue = 15
| date = 1989
| pages = 3759–3777
| doi = 10.1142/S0217751X89001503
| bibcode = 1989IJMPA...4.3759J
}}</ref> the Yang–Baxter equation (YBE) manifested itself in the works of J. B. McGuire<ref>{{cite journal | last=McGuire | first=J. B. | title=Study of Exactly Soluble One‐Dimensional N‐Body Problems | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics | publisher=The American Institute of Physics (AIP) | volume=5 | issue=5 | date=1964-05-01 | issn=0022-2488 | doi=10.1063/1.1704156 | pages=622–636 | bibcode=1964JMP.....5..622M }}</ref> in 1964 and [[C. N. Yang]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Yang | first=C. N. | title=Some Exact Results for the Many-Body Problem in one Dimension with Repulsive Delta-Function Interaction  | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=19 | issue=23 | date=1967-12-04 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1312 | pages=1312–1315 | bibcode=1967PhRvL..19.1312Y }}</ref> in 1967. They considered a quantum mechanical [[many-body problem]] on a line having <math>c\sum_{i<j}\delta(x_i - x_j)</math> as the potential. Using the [[Bethe ansatz]] techniques, they found that the scattering matrix factorized to that of the two-body problem, and determined it exactly. This result established the Yang–Baxter equation as the defining criterion for quantum integrability, linking factorized scattering in one dimension to exactly solvable models.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Faddeev |first=L. D. |title=How Algebraic Bethe Ansatz Works for Integrable Models |journal=Les Houches Lectures on Quantum Symmetries |year=1996 |pages=149–219}}</ref> Here the YBE arises as the consistency condition for the factorization.

In [[statistical mechanics]], the source of the YBE probably goes back to Onsager's star-triangle relation, briefly mentioned in the introduction to his solution of the [[Ising model]]<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Onsager
| first = L.
| title = Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition
| journal = Physical Review
| publisher = Americal Physical Society (APS)
| volume = 65
| issue = 3-4
| date = 1944-02-01
| pages = 117–149
| doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.65.117
| bibcode = 1944PhRv...65..117O
}}</ref> in 1944. The hunt for solvable lattice models has been actively pursued since then, culminating in [[Rodney Baxter]]'s solution of the eight vertex model<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Baxter
| first = R. J.
| title = Partition function of the Eight-Vertex lattice model
| journal = Annals of Physics
| publisher = Elsevier
| volume = 70
| issue = 1
| date = 1972
| pages = 193–228
| issn = 0003-4916
| doi = 10.1016/0003-4916(72)90335-1
| bibcode = 1972AnPhy..70..193B
}}</ref> in 1972.

Another line of development was the theory of factorized ''S''-matrix in two dimensional [[quantum field theory]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Zamolodchikov
| first = Alexander B.
| last2 =  Zamolodchikov
| first2 = Alexey B.
| title = Factorized S-matrices in two dimensions as the exact solutions of certain relativistic quantum field theory models
| journal = Annals of Physics
| publisher = Elsevier
| volume = 120
| issue = 2
| date = 1979
| pages = 253–291
| issn = 0003-4916
| doi = 10.1016/0003-4916(79)90391-9
| bibcode = 1979AnPhy.120..253Z
}}</ref> Alexander B. Zamolodchikov pointed out<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Zamolodchikov
| first = Alexander B.
| title = Z<sub>4</sub>-symmetric factorized S-matrix in two space-time dimensions
| journal = Comm. Math. Phys.
| publisher = Elsevier
| volume = 69
| issue = 2
| date = 1979
| pages = 165–178
| issn = 0003-4916
| doi = 10.1007/BF01221446
| bibcode = 1979CMaPh..69..165Z
}}
</ref> that the algebraic mechanics working here is the same as that in the Baxter's and others' works.

The YBE has also manifested itself in a study of [[Young symmetrizer|Young operators]] in the [[group ring|group algebra]] <math>\mathbb{C} [S_n] </math> of the [[symmetric group]] in the work of [[Algimantas Adolfas Jucys|A. A. Jucys]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Jucys | first=A. A. | title=On the Young operators of the symmetric group | journal=Lietuvos Fizikos Rinkinys | publisher=Gos. Izd-vo Polit. i Nauch. literatury. | volume=6 | date=1966 | pages=163–180 | url=https://www.lietuvos-fizikai.lt/chessidr/straipsniai/LietFizRink/LFR-1966-v6-p179-AlgJucys-On_the_Young_operators_of_the_symmetric_groups.pdf}}</ref> in 1966.

==General form of the parameter-dependent Yang–Baxter equation==
Let <math>A</math> be a [[unital algebra|unital]] [[associative algebra]].  In its most general form, the parameter-dependent Yang–Baxter equation is an equation for <math>R(u,u')</math>, a parameter-dependent element of the [[tensor product of algebras|tensor product]] <math>A \otimes A</math> (here, <math>u</math> and <math>u'</math> are the parameters, which usually range over the [[real number]]s ℝ in the case of an additive parameter, or over [[positive real numbers]] ℝ<sup>+</sup> in the case of a multiplicative parameter).

Let <math>R_{ij}(u,u') = \phi_{ij}(R(u,u'))</math> for <math>1\le i< j \le3</math>, with algebra [[homomorphism]]s <math>\phi_{ij} : A \otimes A \to A \otimes A \otimes A</math> determined by

<math display="block">\phi_{12}(a \otimes b) = a \otimes b \otimes 1,</math>

<math display="block">\phi_{13}(a \otimes b) = a \otimes 1 \otimes b,</math>

<math display="block">\phi_{23}(a \otimes b) = 1 \otimes a \otimes b.</math>

The general form of the Yang–Baxter equation is

<math display="block">R_{12}(u_1,u_2) \ R_{13}(u_1,u_3) \ R_{23}(u_2,u_3) = R_{23}(u_2,u_3) \ R_{13}(u_1,u_3) \ R_{12}(u_1,u_2),</math>

for all values of <math>u_1</math>, <math>u_2</math> and <math>u_3</math>.

=== Parameter-independent form ===
Let <math>A</math> be a unital associative algebra.  The parameter-independent Yang–Baxter equation is an equation for <math>R</math>, an invertible element of the tensor product <math>A \otimes A</math>.  The Yang–Baxter equation is

<math display="block">R_{12} \ R_{13} \ R_{23} = R_{23} \ R_{13} \ R_{12},</math>

where <math>R_{12} = \phi_{12}(R)</math>, <math>R_{13} = \phi_{13}(R)</math>, and <math>R_{23} = \phi_{23}(R)</math>.

=== With respect to a basis ===
Often the unital associative algebra is the [[endomorphism algebra|algebra of endomorphisms]] of a [[vector space]] <math>V</math> over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>k</math>, that is, <math>A = \text{End}(V)</math>. With respect to a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] <math>\{e_i\}</math> of <math>V</math>, the components of the matrices <math>R\in \text{End}(V)\otimes\text{End}(V) \cong \text{End}(V\otimes V)</math> are written <math>R_{ij}^{kl}</math>, which is the component associated to the map <math>e_i\otimes e_j \mapsto e_k\otimes e_l</math>. Omitting parameter dependence, the component of the Yang–Baxter equation associated to the map <math>e_a\otimes e_b\otimes e_c \mapsto e_d \otimes e_e \otimes e_f</math> reads

<math display="block">(R_{12})_{ij}^{de}(R_{13})_{ak}^{if}(R_{23})_{bc}^{jk} = (R_{23})_{jk}^{ef} (R_{13})_{ic}^{dk} (R_{12})_{ab}^{ij}.</math>

==Alternate form and representations of the braid group==
Let <math>V</math> be a [[module (mathematics)|module]] of <math>A</math>, and  <math> P_{ij} = \phi_{ij}(P) </math> .  Let <math>P : V \otimes V \to V \otimes V</math> be the [[linear map]] satisfying <math>P(x \otimes y) = y \otimes x</math> for all <math>x, y \in V</math>. The Yang–Baxter equation then has the following alternate form in terms of <math>\check{R}(u,u') = P \circ R(u,u')</math> on <math>V \otimes V</math>.

<math display="block">(\mathbf{1} \otimes \check{R}(u_1,u_2)) (\check{R}(u_1,u_3)  \otimes \mathbf{1})(\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(u_2,u_3)) =  (\check{R}(u_2,u_3) \otimes \mathbf{1}) ( \mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(u_1,u_3) )  ( \check{R}(u_1,u_2) \otimes \mathbf{1}).</math>

Alternatively, we can express it in the same notation as above, defining <math>\check{R}_{ij}(u,u') = \phi_{ij}(\check{R}(u,u'))</math> , in which case the alternate form is

<math display="block">\check{R}_{23}(u_1,u_2) \ \check{R}_{12}(u_1,u_3) \ \check{R}_{23}(u_2,u_3) = \check{R}_{12}(u_2,u_3) \ \check{R}_{23}(u_1,u_3) \ \check{R}_{12}(u_1,u_2).</math>

In the parameter-independent special case where <math>\check{R}</math> does not depend on parameters, the equation reduces to

<math display="block">(\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R})(\check{R} \otimes \mathbf{1})(\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}) = (\check{R}\otimes \mathbf{1})(\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R})(\check{R}\otimes \mathbf{1}),</math>

and (if <math>R</math> is invertible) a [[group representation|representation]] of the [[braid group]], <math>B_n</math>, can be constructed on <math>V^{\otimes n}</math> by <math>\sigma_i = 1^{\otimes i-1} \otimes \check{R} \otimes 1^{\otimes n-i-1}</math> for <math>i = 1,\dots,n-1</math>.  This representation can be used to determine quasi-invariants of [[braid theory|braids]], [[knot (mathematics)|knots]] and [[link (knot theory)|links]].

==Symmetry==
Solutions to the Yang–Baxter equation are often constrained by requiring the <math>R</math> matrix to be invariant under the action of a [[Lie group]] <math>G</math>. For example, in the case <math>G = GL(V)</math> and <math>R(u,u')\in \text{End}(V\otimes V)</math>, the only <math>G</math>-invariant maps in <math>\text{End}(V\otimes V)</math> are the identity <math>I</math> and the permutation map <math>P</math>. The general form of the <math>R</math>-matrix is then <math>R(u, u') = A(u,u')I + B(u, u')P</math> for scalar functions <math>A, B</math>.

The Yang–Baxter equation is homogeneous in parameter dependence in the sense that if one defines <math>R'(u_i, u_j) = f(u_i, u_j)R(u_i,u_j)</math>, where <math>f</math> is a scalar function, then <math>R'</math> also satisfies the Yang–Baxter equation.

The argument space itself may have symmetry. For example translation invariance enforces that the dependence on the arguments <math>(u, u')</math> must be dependent only on the translation-invariant difference <math>u-u'</math>, while [[scale invariance]] enforces that <math>R</math> is a function of the scale-invariant ratio <math>u/u'</math>.

==Parametrizations and example solutions==
A common ansatz for computing solutions is the difference property, <math>R(u,u') = R(u - u')</math> , where R depends only on a single (additive) parameter. Equivalently, taking logarithms, we may choose the parametrization <math>R(u,u') = R(u/u')</math> , in which case R is said to depend on a multiplicative parameter. In those cases, we may reduce the YBE to two free parameters in a form that facilitates computations:

<math display="block">R_{12}(u) \ R_{13}(u+v) \ R_{23}(v) = R_{23}(v) \ R_{13}(u+v) \ R_{12}(u),</math>

for all values of <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>. For a multiplicative parameter, the Yang–Baxter equation is

<math display="block">R_{12}(u) \ R_{13}(uv) \ R_{23}(v) = R_{23}(v) \ R_{13}(uv) \ R_{12}(u),</math>

for all values of <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>.

The braided forms read as:

<math display="block"> (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(u)) (\check{R}(u + v)  \otimes \mathbf{1})  (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(v)) = (\check{R}(v) \otimes \mathbf{1}) (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(u + v))(\check{R}(u) \otimes \mathbf{1} ) </math>
<math display="block"> (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(u)) (\check{R}(uv)  \otimes \mathbf{1})  (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(v)) = (\check{R}(v) \otimes \mathbf{1}) (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(uv))(\check{R}(u) \otimes \mathbf{1} ) </math>

In some cases, the determinant of <math>R (u) </math> can vanish at specific values of the spectral parameter <math> u=u_{0} </math>. Some <math>R </math> matrices turn into a one dimensional projector at
<math> u=u_{0} </math>. In this case a quantum determinant can be defined {{clarify|reason=If it is useful to the article, it deserves some explanation or resources for readers to learn from.|date=December 2017}}.

=== Example solutions of the parameter-dependent YBE ===
* A particularly simple class of parameter-dependent solutions can be obtained from solutions of the parameter-independent YBE satisfying <math> \check{R}^2 = \mathbf{1} </math>, where the corresponding braid group representation is a permutation group representation. In this case, <math> \check{R}(u) = \mathbf{1} + u  \check{R} </math> (equivalently, <math> R(u) = P + u  P \circ \check{R} </math> ) is a solution of the (additive) parameter-dependent YBE. In the case where <math>\check{R} = P</math> and <math> R(u) = P + u \mathbf{1}</math> , this gives the scattering matrix of the  [[Heisenberg model (quantum)|Heisenberg XXX spin chain]].
* The <math>R</math>-matrices of the evaluation modules of the quantum group <math>U_q(\widehat{sl}(2))</math> are given explicitly by the matrix
<math display="block">
\check{R}(z) = \begin{pmatrix}
        q z - q^{-1}z^{-1} & & & \\
        & q-q^{-1} & z-z^{-1} &\\
        & z-z^{-1} & q-q^{-1} &\\
        & & & q z - q^{-1}z^{-1}
    \end{pmatrix}.
</math>
Then the parametrized Yang–Baxter equation (in braided form) with the multiplicative parameter is satisfied:
<math display="block"> (\mathbf{1}\otimes\check{R}(z)) (\check{R}(zz')  \otimes \mathbf{1})  (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(z')) = (\check{R}(z') \otimes \mathbf{1}) (\mathbf{1}\otimes \check{R}(zz'))(\check{R}(z) \otimes \mathbf{1} ) </math>

=== Classification of solutions ===
There are broadly speaking three classes of solutions: rational, trigonometric and elliptic. These are related to [[quantum group]]s known as the [[Yangian]], [[affine quantum group]]s and [[elliptic algebra]]s respectively.

== Set-theoretic Yang–Baxter equation ==
Set-theoretic solutions were studied by [[Vladimir Drinfeld|Drinfeld]].<ref name="drinfeld">{{cite book |last1=Drinfeld |first1=Vladimir |title=Quantum groups : proceedings of workshops held in the Euler International Mathematical Institute, Leningrad, Fall 1990 |date=1992 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=Berlin |doi=10.1007/BFb0101175 |isbn=978-3-540-55305-2 |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0101175 |access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref> In this case, there is an <math>R</math>-matrix invariant basis <math>X</math> for the vector space <math>V</math> in the sense that the <math>R</math>-matrix maps the induced basis of <math>V\otimes V</math> to itself. This then induces a map <math>r: X\times X \rightarrow X\times X</math> given by restriction of the <math>R</math>-matrix to the basis. The set-theoretic Yang–Baxter equation is then defined using the 'twisted' alternate form above, asserting
<math display=block>(id\times r)(r\times id)(id\times r) = (r\times id)(id\times r)(r \times id)</math>
as maps on <math>X\times X\times X</math>. The equation can then be considered purely as an equation in the [[category of sets]].

=== Examples ===
* <math>R = id</math>.
* <math>R = \tau</math> where <math>\tau(u\otimes v) = v\otimes u</math>, the transposition map.
* If <math>(X, \triangleleft)</math> is a (right) [[shelf (algebra)|shelf]], then <math>r(x,y) = (y, x \triangleleft y)</math> is a set-theoretic solution to the YBE.

== Classical Yang–Baxter equation ==
Solutions to the classical YBE were studied and to some extent classified by [[Alexander Belavin|Belavin]] and Drinfeld.<ref name="bd">{{cite journal |last1=Belavin |first1=A. A. |last2=Drinfel'd |first2=V. G. |title=Solutions of the classical Yang - Baxter equation for simple Lie algebras |journal=Functional Analysis and Its Applications |date=1983 |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=159–180 |doi=10.1007/BF01081585 |s2cid=123126711 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01081585 |access-date=4 February 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Given a 'classical <math>r</math>-matrix' <math>r: V\otimes V \rightarrow V\otimes V</math>, which may also depend on a pair of arguments <math>(u, v)</math>, the classical YBE is (suppressing parameters)
<math display="block">[r_{12}, r_{13}] + [r_{12}, r_{23}] + [r_{13}, r_{23}] = 0</math>
This is quadratic in the <math>r</math>-matrix, unlike the usual quantum YBE which is cubic in <math>R</math>.

This equation emerges from so called quasi-classical solutions to the quantum YBE, in which the <math>R</math>-matrix admits an [[asymptotic expansion]] in terms of an expansion parameter <math>\hbar,</math>
<math display="block">R_\hbar = I + \hbar r + \mathcal{O}(\hbar^2).</math>
The classical YBE then comes from reading off the <math>\hbar^2</math> coefficient of the quantum YBE (and the equation trivially holds at orders <math>\hbar^0, \hbar</math>).
